utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted and Thomas Laugel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just suggested for the record that Your Honours are sitting under Rule 15 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. Indeed, Mr. Zivanovic. Thank you very much. The record should indeed reflect that we are sitting 15 -- pursuant to Rule 15 bis, Judge Mindua being absent. Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Susa, good morning.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, yesterday we talked about your contacts in Ilok with the military authorities. First, I would like to ask you if you personally or as the ministry at any point in time went to Ilok and stayed there?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stayed in Ilok by virtue of the fact that I was a minister. My family also moved to Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain tell us when that was and how that came about?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the winter of 1991. I already had an office in Ilok where I communicated with people. After I met a gentleman by the name of Andrija Islovak [phoen], who was an accountant in Agrokomerc, he asked me if I had a family. And I said, yes, I did, but we were not together. My husband -- my wife and my son were in one place and my parents and my other child were in another place. And then he suggested that I move into his mother-in-law's house. This was an elderly lady. I agreed and we all moved in there. And so for the first time after a number of months my whole family was together again there. It was a house by the road so that there was a constant danger of incidents. My younger son was naughty by nature, and so after a couple of months I moved to the so-called Sokacko Brdo hill. That's where a gentleman used to live. He was a Serb. He left his house. He moved to Australia. The house belonged to a Croat named Mile Zovko. I moved into the house. Mr. Zovko's wife lived in Ilok. Her name was Miluska [phoen]. She was a Slovak. I was in contact with her. I called her and she said: "Please stay in the house. I am glad that you are there and that you are looking after it in this way." I lived in that house until 1997. Very quickly I got in touch with Mr. Mile Zovko as soon as the phone lines were back on, and our contacts were very good and remained very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at P1710, tab 575, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report by the 1st Guards Motorised Division, report of the 31st of December, 1991, following a meeting at the government's commission which was held the day before on the 30th of December. I wanted to ask you this. You've had the opportunity to see the document. Could you please tell us if you remember the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less, I do remember the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the third paragraph, your address is referred to when you said, among other things, that a large number of refugees did not come at the invitation of the government but in an unorganised manner. Is that something that you said at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether any of the military authorities disputed this at the time?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody disputed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that it was the government's wish to maintain accurate records of people who had temporarily occupied homes. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the army kept any records?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they had their records.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It also states here that you didn't want to pre-empt any political solutions for the future and that everything was of a temporary nature. Are you able to tell us whether you did say that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain now what you meant to say by that, that you did not wish to anticipate a political solution?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I'm not mistaken I already spoke about that yesterday or the day before. The arrival of the refugees from the area of Western Slavonia did not mean the definite departure of those people from the Western Slavonia area. We assumed and we wanted those people at some point to return to their homes. We wanted everyone to return to their homes. In that sense, the fact that they were received in the area that we covered was of a temporary nature as assistance to the people in the winter, the winter was just ahead, and so we wanted to provide a roof over their heads. I think I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the last paragraph on this page where the words or some parts of the address were interpreted. These are the words of the Deputy Prime Minister Boro Bogunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution objects to this manner of leading the witness through a document. The witness -- rather than asking the witness open questions about this meeting, Mr. Zivanovic is simply putting a document to this witness in a leading manner and asking him to confirm or deny what was said in this document. The better course would be to ask the witness what he recalls he himself said, what other people at the meeting said, and then at that point raise issues that are in this document. But otherwise, it's completely leading and it's entitled to very little weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The witness already discussed this document and he's familiar with it, but I could rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us if you remember what the position of Mr. Boro Bogunovic was at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that Boro Bogunovic's position was significantly different than my own. I must say that Boro Bogunovic expressed himself in a fairly confused manner, and I'm afraid that whoever drafted the document could not really be specific or precisely define all the things that Boro Bogunovic said. But if we had to come to a final conclusion, I don't think that Boro Bogunovic's position was significantly different from my own. Had it been, it wouldn't have really mattered that much because I was representing the government. I was authorised to state the government's position at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I just note for the record that his answer verifies my concern, which is the leading nature of this document. He's already commenting on what is written here and interpreting what he believes was the reason for it to have what it says in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is noted, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the document now, the last paragraph on that page. Could you please tell us if Boro Bogunovic said at the time that the government wanted to change the structure of the population at any cost?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether Boro Bogunovic insisted that people are settled and placed under intense artillery fire in the zone of intense combat activities?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer because of the interpreters. They didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this entire area, there were no intense combat activities. There were no combat activities at all. So this remark could not have been true, even if it had been said. Let me explain. We were talking about Serb refugees here, so I assume that Boro Bogunovic would not place Serb refugees in intense combat zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at document from the Prosecution's 65 ter list, that's document 62 -- 6028, tab 653.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me if you know if there were any SBWS organs of authority in Lovas at the time-period stated here, the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the fourth paragraph of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in the English it goes to the following page where it said that the town commander stayed in the village of Lovas.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not see the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that he wanted to review the troops and that there was a contact with the commander and the president of the Serbian autonomous region, Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a representative of the Serbian autonomous region who whose name was Savic, in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this man and there was no such function as president of the SAO. The person was obviously misrepresenting himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It states here that this person who was a commander of some unit over there was contacted and he was told that he had to place himself under the Lovas Town Command, otherwise the Ilok command will be disarmed. Could you please tell us: At that time, could the Ilok command do that at that time? Did it have the possibility of doing something like that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The witness's last answer is he doesn't know who this individual is and anything about this, so how can this witness comment on the rest of the paragraph? It could be completely speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it is not good interpretation of the witness answer. The witness answer is that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The witness should repeat his answer then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- he had no such function.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will gladly repeat my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That he doesn't know the man and there was no such function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, just one moment. The witness will repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know Mr. Savic. The position of the president of the SAO did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a member of the government by that name?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: A reference is made to a unit that the gentleman was in command of. I'd like to know whether at that time the command of the town of Ilok had the authority to disband a unit which didn't want to be put under its control.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was its legal obligation. It had to do it under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 6028 will be Exhibit D223.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the government participate in the setting up of the police stations in Ilok, Vukovar, Tovarnik, Mirkovci?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is a very clear report issued by the military about that. It was the military that set up those police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Ministry of Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem appoint commanders or staffs?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up P373, tab 685. I'm interested in the second page of the original, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report dealing with the setting up of the five police stations in the places that I have just mentioned. As you are reading paragraph 2, would you say that this reflects the situation as existed at the time in the area?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how things were. The military influenced the setting up of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now can you look at paragraph 4. A reference is made to dealing with the issues of settling and resettling. How would you explain this wording? What is resettling? What is the issue of resettling that the military reports about in this document?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to ask them. We never dealt with the concept of resettling. We always dealt with the issue of settling. These are different things. We never dealt with the concept of resettling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Under 4, it says that the organ for the civilian issues of this command is confronted with the issues of settling and resettling. Did you hear from them what you meant?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been very good if they had presented that problem to us either in a written or a verbal form. They never did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If we skip the following paragraph, we will come to the next one where a reference is made to the self-styled representatives of the authorities of the Serbian region. When the government heard from the military that some people turned up and introduced themselves as the representatives of the government, how did you react?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were never informed about that. It is very strange that some people are referred to as "self-styled government representatives" and no names are mentioned. The military knew who they were. They should have mentioned their names in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please bear with me. I would like to call up document 379 under tab 661.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, can counsel please repeat the number? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I call up the document, I have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about the area of Ilok and surrounding villages. Who set up the staffs and units of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Belic says in his report that it was the military that did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P379, tab 661.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here, inter alia, that TO units and staffs in towns are in the process of being established. This is what we read in paragraph 1. Could you please tell me whether this reflects what you knew at the time?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. As I'm reading this text, I can see that they were being set up by the military. That's what I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were the justice minister. Did you issue a binding instruction about the work of the commissions for temporary settlement?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't do it as the justice minister. I did it as a government member in charge of that issue. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document under tab 577. It's on the Prosecutor's 65 ter list under number 6115.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether this is the instruction that you issued?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us in more detail what you meant by this instruction when it comes to the contracts on the exchange of assets and property with citizens of Croatian ethnicity. Why did you say that those contracts should be considered null and void and that they cannot have any legally binding consequences?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course during a war or an imminent threat of war, I thought that conditions were not in place for all the parties to be equal when contracts were being signed. Let me illustrate that by an example. When a Serb came to a Croat and said, "I want to sign an agreement with you to exchange our properties," in my view such an agreement would be null and void because it could be assumed that a Croat accepted that under duress. In the times of war or imminent threat of war, there can be no conventional exchange or sale of property at all. So this was the gist of that binding instruction that I issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that the consequences of any exchange or sale of property that happened after the 25th of September should be considered null and void. Is that for the same reasons or some other reasons?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is for the same reasons because according to the information that we had, their contracts had already been signed on the exchange of assets under suspicious conditions. We did not want to participate in any of that because we believed that the consequences of such legal transactions at some point would be huge and maybe even irreparable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 6115 becomes Exhibit D224.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Once the commission was set up by the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, did the Yugoslav People's Army, i.e. the command of the town of Ilok, continue to participate in dealing with the issue of settling refugees in the area?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the time. Until the moment the JNA withdrew from the area, they were involved in the settlement, and I won't say that they participated in the resettlement, of individuals in the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, the command of the town of Ilok, i.e., the military personnel in charge of those issues, were they in direct communication with local civilian authorities or did that communication go via the government?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in very direct communication with everybody. They bypassed us in everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they issue any instructions, orders, or any such thing to those local bodies of authority?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up P2280 under tab 663.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report by the command of the town of Ilok, dating to March 1992. Under 7, which is the last paragraph, it says that the commander of the town held a meeting with presidents of local communes, Territorial Defence Staff commanders, and other responsible officials to discuss the tasks assigned to them by the 1st Motorised Corps command. Were you invited to such a meeting as members of the commission that was in charge of Ilok? You were no longer in the government at that time.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. But there were other people, and they were not invited to such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next page, page 3. In English it would be the previous page. In fact, it would be the last page in English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This report lists questions that require urgent answers regarding the community of Ilok, and you have a list of places. In the first question we see: "What is the status of new settlers, what does it entail? This is the biggest problem," et cetera. Did the military authorities ever address the government with these questions, asking for answers or maybe consulting you about this?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not with me, but I can't say whether they tried with somebody else. I never received such a list of questions to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear from any of your colleagues in the government that the military authorities had addressed them with such issues?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say I don't know, that means I've never heard of such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it seems I did not ask the tendering of the previous document into evidence. It is from tab 577.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And I would tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And the number is, for the Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is exhibit number from the Rule 65 ter Prosecution list 6115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number was already admitted and marked as D224.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us to the best of your knowledge, was this area ever visited by international observers?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They did not have any contact with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will come back to a couple of documents about this, but now I'd like to move on to the period after the creation of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Would you be able to tell me, if you know, whether you were involved in the writing of the constitution of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of us from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was involved in the writing of the constitution of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in its original form as it was adopted in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember for what territory this constitution of the RSK was written?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you, because it was very obvious, it said: Only for the territory of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see tab 591, L3. In English could we look at paragraph -- Article 3, in English. It's the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is Article 3 that you have discussed.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember, under this constitution, what did the election of the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina look like? How did it happen?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Direct general elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, according to that constitution, who elected the government and to whom was the government answerable?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government was answerable to the president and the assembly. At the proposal of the assembly, the prime minister and other ministers' designates were appointed. The president was able to replace or dismiss the prime minister designate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in the writing of amendments to the constitution?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did these amendments to the constitution change this Article 3 that regard the territory of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it had to be changed because the RSK was not only created for the territory of Krajina but also Western Slavonia and Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. These three regions practically joined together to form the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at L5, that's tab 593.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is in the first amendment.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amendment 1, para 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did this amendment practically include the region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem into the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at the third amendment. It's on the same page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now tell us what arrangements were made for the election of the president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was elected by the assembly. But you can see that from the previous amendment, amendment 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at amendment 2, then, on the same page of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Under this amendment, the assembly not only elects and dismisses the president but also oversees his work. Was that the same arrangement as in the previous version?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, did these amendments change anything in the responsibility of the president towards the assembly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the second institution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now he was responsible only to the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see in which amendment it is stipulated?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could make this text a little larger, I could see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we should move to the next page in English. Could we zoom in on the next amendment in the original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now you can see it. From the amendment 4, para 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what was the constitutional position of the president of the republic vis-à-vis the Serbian army of Krajina? Did it remain the same as in the constitution or was it changed?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the previous constitution?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the constitution as it was adopted. These are amendments.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It changed. Now the president could propose the commander of the Territorial Defence but he was no longer able to replace him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at L55, tab 625.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you could look at amendment 8.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Para 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that one. According to para 3, the president of the republic appoints the commander of the Territorial Defence. At that time when this amendment was passed, and it was in May 1992, was the commander of the Territorial Defence in fact the command of the Serbian -- no, no, I made a mistake. The commander of the Territorial Defence, was he already appointed?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in the writing of these amendments to the constitution, amendments 1 through 8?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But not in this form. This is the final language adopted. The proposed language was quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us exactly what was different between the proposals and the final version?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our proposal did not take into account the still great powers of Milan Babic in SAO Krajina. The first constitution was written for him. But when Goran Hadzic came into power, then all these amendments were necessary, and they all knew it, but at the same time they insisted that some of the amendments be rendered null and void and replaced by these amendments which are not quite appropriate. They explained it by saying, and I could accept it, by saying that the first version envisaged elections of the president by general direct elections and thus was entitled to great powers, whereas in the new version the president was elected solely by the assembly and therefore his scope of powers should be smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the constitutional powers of the president of the republic with further amendments, were they narrowed, did they remain the same, were they expanded?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were successively slowly being narrowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember if any constitutional amendments were adopted that would change the way in which the president of the republic was elected?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was at a later stage when, again, we had political turbulence in the Republic of Serbian Krajina and when one could assume that some other people were pretenders for the presidential post who again felt that they would easily win the direct general election. I can specifically say that this refers to Mr. Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at tab 638. This is 1D3761.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You can see that this is the 29th of October -- or, actually, September of 1992. Can you please tell us how this amendment came about, amendment 10 specifically? This is an amendment that you already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please enlarge the text? I don't see it very well. Yes, this is what I was talking about earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mention Mr. Martic. Could you briefly tell us what was the relationship between Mr. Martic and Goran Hadzic in this period from the elections, from the time when Goran Hadzic was elected as president of the Serbian Krajina onwards?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, in respect of all of us that were appointed to certain posts and located in the Knin area, there was a kind of mistrust and it was difficult for us to do our job for several reasons. One of them is the long and difficult road in order to get there at all. And secondly, a part of their bodies was in a very chaotic state. So everything was quite difficult. That is how Goran Hadzic was received as well. Most of the population of the SAO Krajina, the former SAO Krajina, did not forgive him for the fact that he, they felt, got Milan Babic out of the game in a very strange way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please clarify that what you mean, that he threw Milan Babic out of the game?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because before the Serbian regions were formed and became the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, the favourite person to win the presidential post of this new Republic of Serbian Krajina, judging by his popularity and the media promotion, was Babic. After Milan Babic definitely indicated that he would not accept the Vance Plan at any cost, it was understood that he, as a crucial political factor, had to be pushed out of the game, and he was replaced by Goran Hadzic in the only possible way, by being elected by the assembly, because then he would not even have managed to win the direct general election. In the Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem area, we had a smaller population in relation to the SAO Krajina. We were not well known and it was normal that their politicians would win more votes in any general election in which the majority of the population would take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us what was the actual influence of Goran Hadzic, especially in that area? In the Knin Krajina, in the SAO Krajina, what was his political influence in the period when he was the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid it was not very great. If you look at his narrowed powers, he did not really have too much authority according to the laws and the regulations, and he did not impose himself. He didn't politically engage himself in that area. He would stay there for as long as he needed to and then he would return to the SBWS area. This is something that was well known, so he really never gained much popularity over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Goran Hadzic lived in that period?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He lived in Novi Sad during that whole period. That was where his family was. We were all neither here nor there throughout that whole period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When were you elected into the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Goran was elected president at an assembly session in Borovo Selo, I was elected justice minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at L6, please. This is tab 594.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see the decision on the screen now. It states that it was adopted on the 26th of February, 1992. I wanted to ask you something else. I see that the prime minister was elected here as well as 13 other ministers of that government. Could you please tell us, were any ministries left open? Some ministers were perhaps not appointed at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were not appointed because we tried to have equal representation throughout that whole area, and certain areas simply at that time did not have the people that they could propose for those ministerial posts. There were four or five ministries left unfilled here and their posts were filled later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can see that the culture ministry was left without a minister. No culture minister was appointed at that time. Are you able to tell us if you know whether somebody was appointed later and who was that?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Sergej Veselinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the government in the beginning after the elections adopted any principled directives or conclusions about its work, adopted any goals?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did draw conclusions about its goals. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at P3055, please. This is tab 632.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness is shown this document, perhaps the next question should have been what those goals were. Because it could be interesting to know if this witness has any independent recollection of those goals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, it seems reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would ask the witness just to identify the document, if it was the document what he spoke about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, could you please look at this document. This is the declaration on the political goals of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and it says here that it was adopted on the 18th of May, 1992. Could you please tell us whether this is a document setting out the political goals of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. We don't have to read the document but I will give you the main points of the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The declaration boils down to a definitive assertion which people perhaps didn't understand initially, and that is that all of our work, our desires, our -- at joining Yugoslavia again should end. We said that in an indirect but understandable way, saying that we will maintain relations with the former Yugoslavia that are guided by common goals and objectives. This is something that people perhaps didn't understand, but to me - and I participated in the drafting of the declaration - it was clear what the main elements were. Everything else there that is contained in the declaration is of a declaratory nature and it's not so significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think you already said that but that was my question: Did you take part in the drafting of the declaration?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did anything in the declaration indicate that the goal of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina was the creation of something that could be described as Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the declaration and the political position that we found ourselves in, we could have written whatever we wanted. But it was clear that nothing would come of that goal, and I didn't really believe that it existed anymore. I successively took part in all of the declarations from the SBWS one to others, and we always emphasized that basic desire to remain in Yugoslavia. However, with this declaration we definitely abandoned that idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not ask to tender into evidence document 1D3761. It is tab 638. It is amendment -- amendments on the constitution of the RSK. It was shown to the witness. Amendments 9, 10, and 11. And I would tender it. I'm sorry for the inconveniences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D3761 becomes Exhibit D225.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, these are amendments to the constitution. Amendments --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To the constitution of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Should --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The amendments number 9, 10, and 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Shouldn't we give them an L number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Rather than a --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- rather than a D number? Madam Registrar, could you provide an L number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next L number will be L69 and D225 remains available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, you took part in the talks on the Vance Plan. You spoke about that yesterday. Do you recollect one of the elements of the Vance Plan being the return of refugees?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that was one of the key elements of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And how did you understand that part of the Vance Plan? Who was supposed to come back and where?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the people that had left their hearths, whatever the circumstances, who had left their homes, mostly, and this was something that was known, were fleeing from the destruction of war and all the ills that war brought; thus, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that you gave statements to the media on these matters?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I provided many statements to the media on this topic as well, among others. I really don't know how many times I addressed the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 1D3645, tab 558.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a statement, I think, given to the Novi Sad Dnevnik on the 20th of March, 1992. It was less than a month after you were elected into the government of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the text: "Krajina, Never Again in Croatia."

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that and I was afraid as soon as I saw the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, my records indicate that this has not been added to the Defence's 65 ter exhibit list. Can that be confirmed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is 1D3645. It was on our Rule 65 ter list and I think that it is on our list, too. Our list for this witness, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think you mentioned the tab number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The tab number is 558.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe this is still subject to a pending motion by the Defence, the third motion to amend its Rule 65 ter list. And this -- I don't believe this was one that was brought up at the beginning of this witness's testimony. This wasn't included in Mr. Zivanovic's oral submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can double-check it and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You'll let us know after --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- and see after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, did it deal with the return of refugees and displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did it issue documents? Did it pass decisions or some other enactments to that effect?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, decisions were passed both by the government and the assembly. The government issued decisions, the assembly issued declarations. We spoke about that in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up under tab 561. This is an exhibit from the Prosecutor's 65 ter list, 1099. [In English] No, no. [Interpretation] It was below that. Declaration. [In English] The document on the top of the original. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do we have an English translation of this declaration? I only see a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that there is a translation, but if not I'll withdraw the question. Thank you. May we see L8, please. It is tab 596.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You already spoke about a document which was issued by the assembly and we will not be looking at that; however, we are going to look at a decision that was passed by the government. What you see on the screen now, is that the decision in question? It was issued on the 21st of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether refugees and displaced persons returned in keeping with this decision?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why? Why did they not return in accordance with this decision?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody prevented the refugees from returning. We encouraged their return as much as we could. However, in conversations with the people on the other side, we realised that they did not demonstrate any wish to return for as long as we existed as an authority. In other words, that they would wait for the Croatian authorities to be re-established after which they would be willing to return to their homes. On our side, we did our utmost to start the return of refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to this decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can the original be zoomed in just a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In Article 1, it says that all those who wanted to return are required to send a written request to the secretariat of the interior in charge, depending on their previous place of residence. Were such requests filed at all?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say that this did not happen, not even once, because I don't know. In any case, the number of such applications was not significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This decision also envisages a possibility to ban certain people from returning. Who could have been forbidden to return?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only those for which there was evidence that they participated in the commission of crimes until the moment it could be established for a fact whether those crimes were committed or not in a legally binding procedure. We didn't want to harm those people because otherwise they would have had to come, be detained, and wait for the court decision to become final. I believe that this was fair on our behalf. In respect of the other side which arrested a lot of people and kept them detained for a long time before it was finally established that they were innocent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Zivanovic. We'll take our first break, 30 minutes. We will be back at 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness enters the courtroom, I would ask the Trial Chamber to admit on our Rule 65 ter list the document -- document 1D3645. This document was among the documents filed with our third motion to amend our Rule 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is article that I tried to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, and I believe we -- we raised this in our response to that motion. We object to the admission of this document, which is an open source document, a publication that could have been found by the Defence at any time in these proceedings. And I would note that the Defence has met with this witness since at least September 2013 and certainly could have been apprised of this open source newspaper article well in advance of their case or at least by the beginning of their case, and now we're several months into their case and they're proposing to add it to the list and we oppose it on due diligence grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that it is in the interests of justice to admit this document and it is relevant for this particular witness, actually. It is his statement to the media as to the return of refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. The document can be added to the 65 ter list and is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 1D3645 will be Exhibit D225.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, sorry. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, we started talking about your statement which you gave to the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D3645 under tab 558. Can we zoom in on the original, please. Under the title: "Krajina, Never Again In Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your words are quoted regarding the return of refugees. You will find them in the first column towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say, inter alia, that: "The return of Croats to Krajina is a normal process which we will not try to stop in any way because we will not accept the policy of citizens of the first and second class." Did you ever give such a statement to this particular newspaper or newspapers in general?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt that these are my words, because I did give such statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether this statement reflected the position of the government and the authorities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina at that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I conveyed the positions of my government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know what were the problems confronted by the refugees who wanted to return to either of the sides?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The return on both sides was a painstaking process. There was mistrust on both sides about the return of the other side. I have to say that in principle we were in favour of a return and we would have done it gladly, but there were no invitations to people to return and there were no technical capabilities in place for our people to return to Croatia. Most of the Croatian assets in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, including the largest part of Krajina that I was familiar with, was protected and preserved. That was my priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us a bit more specifically about that problem; namely, that there were no invitations to people to return and that technical capabilities were lacking for the return of people to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the same time as we were making decisions and declarations and appealing to Croats to return to their homes via mass media, there were no similar invitations from the other side to Serbs to return, at this time, only to the area of Western Slavonia. And the whole tragedy is that such invitations were not made, and even if they had been made, they could not have been taken up because numerous settlements and houses had already been burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in any discussions with international representatives or the Croatian side about this issue of having resettled persons returned?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I participated on a number of occasions in talks with representatives of the international community. More specifically, the international community organised discussions between us and the Croatian side and there was a period in which these talks were held very intensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the reason why Croat refugees did not return to their homes in Ilok and that area of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. How would the witness know that? At the very least, there has to be some foundation laid so we can understand what the basis of his answer would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I see, the witness said that he participated in discussions between -- with the Croatian side about the -- about the resettled person -- about the persons returns. It was my previous question and witness answer. And I asked him if he knows anything about the one specific local -- area, about Ilok, and where he testified that he was one of the government representatives for such matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, Mr. Zivanovic is therefore missing a number of questions before he can get to the question that he asked. He's simply not laying the foundation and, I suggest, leading the witness right to the point he's trying to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the previous answers of the witness is about Ilok and about -- and his last answers gave enough of a foundation for this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Zivanovic. The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need. I understand both you and the Prosecutor. If you mean whether I talked directly to Croats who wanted to return to Ilok, that did not happen. But through their representatives who talked to us under the aegis of the United Nations, I understood that they were insisting at all costs that the organs of Croatian authorities be established first, and I understood it as a precondition for their return set by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that they insisted on the establishment of Croatian authorities, you mean which territory?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area I know best and the one that's closest to me is Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. The Republic of Serbian Krajina was not covered so extensively in all its parts in the negotiations, so I can't know what happened exactly in Glina, Banja, Kordun, Lika, or Dalmatia, but I know very well what was going on in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender the document 1D3645 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's the document that was admitted at the start of this session --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- and added to the 65 ter list as D225.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, I will now go back to a document that I was not able to show you earlier, but first of all, I have a question. Do you remember during your tenure on that commission for Ilok, for short, do you remember whether you received any requests from the local commune of Mohovo?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I received one request from Mohovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was this request about, if you remember, before I show you the document?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must tell you straight away why I remember it, because it was the only local commune that came directly to me for advice and for consultation about the situation in that local commune, so it's not difficult to remember. From earlier, I knew two of the three members of that small delegation that came to Ilok to present their problem. Mohovo, and I knew that from before, was a mixed community of Hungarians, Ukrainians, Ruthenians, and Serbs, and some refugees had also temporarily settled there under the supervision of the army. In and of itself that was not a problem. It wouldn't have been a problem if it hadn't disrupted not only interethnic but also interpersonal relations. So there we had a problem not only between Serbs and Croats but between everybody. And the army contributed to it by encouraging the moving out of Croats and all the others, whereas the local residents of Mohovo wanted to stop it. I understood that they had first addressed the army, asking them for protection and for diffusion of tensions, but it didn't happen. In that village before the JNA came, there were ethnic Croats who had received weapons and boasted about it, and now they were denying they had weapons. These people were committed to preserving their little village, and they asked me what I thought about it - "I," meaning the government of SBWS - whether I was able to mediate in their relations with the army, and whether there was a way to give them full control over resolving the problems in the village. I did that and within the next few days I invited them again. There was no post office working at that time, and I told them the position of the government; namely, that we do not encourage any emigration, that all places within SBWS were equal. I had spoken to the army which promised me that all the steps would be taken to stabilise the situation, and in that way I kind of agreed with them that they are the best placed to resolve the issues in their village. These people were a tight-knit community. They were not only friends but they were also related to each other. So that's what I told them and, of course, I did not attach any strings to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware at that time of the position of the army - that is to say, a specific command of the JNA - regarding the ethnic composition or possibly a change of the ethnic picture of the population in that area of Ilok and its surroundings?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite truthful, I cannot say that anyone told me directly that they were in favour of people moving out. However, from their internal documents I realised that they were very interested and very involved in it, and they were exchanging reports between them, reports saying how many people moved in or out and what activities needed to be carried out to get people to move out in even greater numbers and how to change the ethnic structure of particular places.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at P1715. That's tab 679.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a report from a meeting held on 21st February 1992. It was held, as you see, in Mirkovci, and we see who was present at the meeting including the representatives of local authorities. Did you or any member of the government or any member of that commission get the invitation to this meeting, this meeting between local authorities and the military?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we had been invited, we would have come. We always did. But I don't see any of us here, so I can only conclude that we were not invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We don't see the names of all the people who attended. We only see various job titles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can look at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We see that the meeting was chaired by Corps Commander General Delic, which seems to indicate that he was also present. I'm interested in item 5 (a). It says the agency for civilian affairs, meaning a member of the JNA. It says that at the level of the government of SBWS, measures need to be taken to resolve the issue of settling currently uninhabited places, Nijemci, Apsevci, et cetera, as soon as possible, and that in places that are settled, the ethnic structure should be changed more efficiently. They are suggesting that the government should do this. Has such a request ever been made of the government to change the ethnic structure more efficiently?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never suggested anything of the sort to us. And if they had, we wouldn't have accepted. Mr. Delic cannot speak on behalf of the government or suggest anything to the government because he is not a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm not talking about the government but about some members of the army. Did they hold such a view?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously. It's written here. That's what I was talking about. There are many such documents, including at lower levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, you spoke earlier about the judiciary of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and later you yourself were a minister of justice in the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. First we'll discuss Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. What were the competencies of the judiciary at the time when the Yugoslav People's Army with their military commands and staffs were present there?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our jurisdiction was narrowed down considerably. The army had powers according to the legislation that governed immediate threat of war. So they were in charge of taking pre-investigating, investigating, and prosecuting measures in a large number of cases. We did not interfere, but we also noticed that a number of cases was also ending up before our courts. So we concluded that there must be some instruction from military commands that the civilian police or military police under their command should submit some cases to our judiciary and those were, as a rule, less serious crimes, and we prosecuted them. This continued until the JNA withdrew. After that, our courts were showered by a great number of cases that had previously been handled by the military judiciary, and that included everything, aggravated robberies, thefts, killings, murders, et cetera, and we started dealing with this intensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the immediate threat of war. Do you perhaps remember when the immediate threat of war was declared?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The immediate threat of war was declared in October 1991, if I'm not mistaken. It was published in the Official Gazette of the SFRY. I think that it went into effect on the 18th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at P2932. This is tab 711.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the first document published in this issue of this Official Gazette. It states that the immediate threat of war was established on the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but it goes into effect on the day it is published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in another thing. You said that military organs had certain judicial responsibilities when imminent danger of war was declared. So what I'm interested in is: Did you know about this? Did you have an opportunity to see the document or to hear of it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we received all the Official Gazettes. They were dispatched to all the official organs that were dealing with state, social affairs. They were also dispatched to all work organisations. So it was an obligation to know all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at 1D2481, tab 488.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a draft record from a session of the Presidency of the SFRY of the 5th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It states here that the order has been given --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please tell us where he's reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- if this order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- the interpreters are asking you whether you could tell them where you're reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can read the first paragraph of the original, where it says that: At the proposal of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence and with consultation with members of the SFRY Presidency, the SFRY Presidency, without holding a session, issued the order on the territorial jurisdiction of first-degree military courts and military prosecutor's offices at military commands. And that the order also determines the competencies of military courts in the event of an imminent threat of war. What I would like to know is if you know whether this order that had to do with competencies of military courts in the event of an imminent threat of war was applied in the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem as of October 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, how could he -- the witness answer that question without seeing the order, if there was one. But I guess he already answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we don't have the order but we have the minutes from this -- from the session of this organ of the former Yugoslavia. And in many cases the minutes from these organs were admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the issue is foundation. There is no foundation that this witness attended this meeting. We have no idea what were the contents of this order. So for this witness to testify that this order was, in fact, adopted or implemented, he simply cannot -- it would be speculation without further foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't ask the witness whether he was present at the session of the Presidency of SFRY, but I just ask him whether he knows that the jurisdiction of the military courts were implemented in the SBWS during the immediate threat of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And did you ask whether there was -- there was -- there had been issued the order you were referring to? Mr. Olmsted's first -- yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. My question is whether this jurisdiction of the military courts as presented in this document was implemented on the territory of the SBWS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, again, Your Honours, that goes back to my question: As we don't know what the order is, it doesn't -- the document doesn't mention anything about the SBWS, so the witness simply cannot answer these questions without speculating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is -- it is stated here that the order also determines the competencies of military courts in the event of an immediate threat of war. It is a -- this paragraph, the second -- the second sentence in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Zivanovic. So the witness should answer that question, whether he knows whether this is implemented in a certain territory which you may or may -- which you may define.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I define -- I asked about the territory of the SBWS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Then put a clear question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susa, are you able to tell us whether starting from October 1991, the military courts' competencies applied in the SBWS in the event of immediate threat of war?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will be very co-operative and perhaps I would answer: If I was asked whether I ever saw such an order, I can say I did not. But on the other hand, it is quite clear that military judicial organs behaved in such a way that it could be easily concluded that such an order existed, and it's not possible to avoid the determination of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia by the military organs. They had to apply that in practice. As to what form and under what orders, that is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution objects. The witness's last answer clearly establishes that he is not aware of any such order. He can only presume based upon what he's observing on the ground that maybe such an order was issued, but with regard to this document, he knows nothing about an order that was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, but the witness said that he never saw -- never seen this order, not that he doesn't know anything about this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. The document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D2481 will be Exhibit D226.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you able to tell us until the military courts had the competencies to prosecute the crimes committed in the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, until what time?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the whole period until the army withdrew and until this measure about the declaration of an imminent threat of war was no longer valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when the immediate threat of war ceased to be valid?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime in May or June 1992. There is also a decision on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at P181. This is tab 689.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, on the basis of this, when the decision on the existence of an immediate threat of war was rendered null and void?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you can see the date when it went into effect. That's the date at the top, the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about an incident in Lovas at the so-called minefield where there were a number of Croat inhabitants of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who carried out an investigation into this incident?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning it was the military police that conducted the first actions regarding this investigation, and then later it was handed over to the military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see please 1D157. It is tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a statement by one of the commanders of one of the units that was deployed in Lovas. All I would like to know is if you are aware --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is on the second page. Can we look at the second page of the original, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where the units that took part in this are mentioned and where the person who signed the document reports that he informed the authorised bodies about the incident - i.e., the commander of the Territorial Defence in Serbia, General Djokic - and that he also informed the organs of the 1st Guards Division where the incident occurred. What I would like to know is whether the army ever informed you about this incident, i.e., the judicial organs of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem or later the Republic of Serbian Krajina, so that they could take up the case and prosecute it?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This case was never passed to us for further processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me if it was the 1st Guards Division that was responsible for prosecuting the incident where the incident took place and which reports to the republican staff of the TO of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He addressed the organs properly and he spoke the truth. In the last sentence he says that he informed the authorised person that the investigation is being carried out by organs of the 1st Guards Division, and that was within their competence to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's we go back to the first page, please, in the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You will see in the third paragraph from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This will be the fourth paragraph from the bottom of the page in the English translation -- or, rather, the fourth and the fifth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says that: From the 2nd Motorised Brigade command, it was suggested that the above incident falls within the competencies of the security organ and the 1st Guards Brigade and that it was not my responsibility because it took place in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Motorised Brigade. Does that tally with what you knew about the competencies for such crimes?

utterances.speaker: VOJIN SUSA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you what division, what brigade, because those things mean nothing to me. However, in principle it was the JNA that was responsible and how they distributed responsibilities and competencies among themselves, I wouldn't be able to tell you because I don't know.
